notes.b: A reaction at equilibrium (reactants turning into products at exactly the rate products turn back into reactants, so the amounts stay constant) can be disturbed. Le Châtelier’s principle lets you predict how it responds.
points: Le Châtelier’s principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system responds so as to oppose the change, and a new equilibrium is set up.
A shift to the right means the forward reaction is favoured, so more products form until equilibrium is restored; a shift to the left means more reactants form.
The principle predicts the direction of the shift, not how fast it happens or how large it is; the change is only partly reversed, so the system never fully cancels the disturbance.
notes.tip: Don’t say the system removes the change completely; it only partly opposes it. State the principle in full, including the words ‘a new equilibrium is set up’.

notes.b: Concentration (the amount of a substance per unit volume of solution) is the easiest disturbance to picture. The equilibrium shifts to use up whatever has been added, or to replace whatever has been taken away.
points: Adding a reactant (or removing a product) shifts the equilibrium to the right, using up some of the added reactant and forming more product.
Adding a product (or removing a reactant) shifts the equilibrium to the left, because the system opposes the extra product by turning some of it back into reactant.
Kc (the equilibrium constant, the fixed ratio of product to reactant concentrations in the Kc expression) is unchanged: the concentrations adjust until that ratio is back at its old value.
Removing a product as it forms keeps pulling the equilibrium to the right, so the reaction keeps making more product. This is how a yield (the amount of product obtained) is raised.
In esterification (an alcohol reacting with an acid to make an ester), using an excess of ethanol, the cheaper reactant, shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield of ester.
In Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) (red), adding either reactant deepens the red colour because more of the red product forms. There is more on this in Investigation: disturbing an equilibrium.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to predict and explain the effect of a concentration change on a given equilibrium. Say which way it shifts and why, and remember that Kc does not change.

notes.b: Pressure only affects equilibria that involve gases, because only gases take up very different volumes depending on how many molecules there are. The equilibrium shifts to the side that exerts less pressure when pressure is raised.
points: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas, because that side exerts the lower pressure; decreasing the pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas.

Count only the gas molecules, using the coefficients (the numbers in front of each formula): N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) has 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so high pressure shifts it to the right, giving more ammonia.
If both sides have the same number of moles of gas, pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium, e.g. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), with 2 mol on each side.

Compressing H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI makes the purple colour deeper because every concentration, including that of I₂, rises (the same amount of gas is squeezed into a smaller volume); the percentage of each substance is unchanged.
2NO₂(g) (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) (colourless): compressing the mixture in a sealed syringe makes it darker at once, because the concentration of the brown NO₂ rises.
The darkening then fades as the equilibrium shifts to the right, from 2 mol to 1 mol of gas, but the mixture does not become as pale as before.
A change of pressure does not change Kc.
notes.tip: Pressure only matters when the numbers of moles of gas differ, so count gas moles only. For a coloured gas mixture, give the immediate darkening first and then the shift.

notes.b: Heat behaves like a reactant or a product: an exothermic reaction (one that releases heat, ΔH negative) gives out heat, and an endothermic one (ΔH positive) absorbs it. Changing the temperature moves the equilibrium to oppose the change in heat.
points: Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which absorbs heat; lowering it shifts the equilibrium in the exothermic direction, which releases heat.
If the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative), heating shifts the equilibrium to the left and cooling shifts it to the right; the reverse is true if the forward reaction is endothermic.
Example: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), with ΔH about −57 kJ mol⁻¹. Heating shifts the equilibrium to the left, giving a darker brown mixture with more NO₂.
Cooling the same mixture in ice-water shifts the equilibrium to the right, giving a paler mixture because more colourless N₂O₄ forms.
Temperature is the only one of these disturbances that changes Kc: for an exothermic forward reaction Kc falls as temperature rises; for an endothermic one it rises.
Diagram: two sealed tubes of the brown mixture, one in hot water and one in ice-water, each labelled with its colour.
notes.tip: Only temperature changes Kc. Exams ask for the colour change on heating or cooling a coloured gas equilibrium, so work out which direction is exothermic first.

notes.b: A catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up) is not a disturbance to an equilibrium at all, so it cannot shift one.
points: A catalyst does not disturb an equilibrium or change its position, because it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.
A catalyst lets equilibrium be reached more quickly, so the same yield is obtained in less time.
A catalyst does not change Kc.
notes.tip: If a question asks the effect of adding a catalyst on an equilibrium, the answer is no change in position or yield. A catalyst does not shift an equilibrium at all.

notes.b: Le Châtelier’s principle explains familiar things, from the fizz in a drink to the damage that extra carbon dioxide does to sea life. In each case, work out what was disturbed and which way the equilibrium moves.
points: Fizzy drinks: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq). Opening the bottle lowers the pressure of CO₂ above the drink, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and gas bubbles out.
A cold drink holds more dissolved CO₂.
Oceans: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq); CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq); H₂CO₃(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) ⇌ 2HCO₃⁻(aq). Here H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid and CO₃²⁻ is the carbonate ion.
More CO₂ in the air increases the dissolved CO₂ and carbonic acid; the third equilibrium shifts to the right, using up carbonate ions. This is ocean acidification.
With less carbonate available, shellfish and corals find it harder to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.
Indicators: the colour of an acid–base indicator (a dye that changes colour with acidity) changes because adding acid or base shifts HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻. There is more on this in How indicators work.
notes.tip: You may be asked to explain, using Le Châtelier’s principle, the effect of more CO₂ on carbonate in seawater and on shell-making. Follow the chain through the three equilibria to the loss of carbonate.

notes.h: Optimising yield: the Haber process (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Le Châtelier’s principle tells you which conditions give the most ammonia at equilibrium, but cost and rate force compromises.
points: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Ammonia is used mainly to make fertilisers.

Pressure: there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so high pressure increases the yield by Le Châtelier’s principle, and also increases the rate because the concentrations are higher.
In practice a pressure of about 200 atm (range about 150–300 atm) is used as a compromise.
Higher pressures would give more ammonia, but a plant that can withstand them is very expensive to build and run, and the risk of leaks and explosions increases.
Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield at equilibrium. But at low temperature the reaction is too slow to be economic.
In practice a compromise of about 400–500 °C (about 450 °C) gives a reasonable yield at a fast enough rate.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the conditions that give the best yield of ammonia and why the conditions used industrially are a compromise. Le Châtelier alone predicts very high pressure and low temperature, which are not used. Don’t describe the plant in detail.

notes.h: The Haber process: catalyst and ammonia removal (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Two more features keep the Haber process economic: a catalyst that makes the reaction fast enough, and the removal of ammonia so that the equilibrium keeps moving right.
points: The iron catalyst does not change the yield; it lets equilibrium be approached quickly at the compromise temperature.

Ammonia is removed by cooling and liquefying it, which keeps pulling the equilibrium to the right, and unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the catalyst, so the overall conversion is high.
notes.tip: You may be asked for the role of the iron catalyst: it speeds up reaching equilibrium and does not change the yield.

notes.h: Optimising yield: the Contact process (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Contact process makes sulfur trioxide, the step on the way to sulfuric acid. It follows the same pattern as the Haber process: Le Châtelier predicts one set of conditions and practice uses another.
points: Contact process (sulfuric acid manufacture): 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH about −197 kJ mol⁻¹.
Le Châtelier predicts high pressure (3 mol of gas on the left, 2 mol on the right) and low temperature for the best yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic.
In practice about 450 °C is used as a compromise between yield and rate, with a vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst.
The pressure is only slightly above atmospheric (1–2 atm), because the yield is already very high and extra pressure would cost more than it gains.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the conditions for the best yield of sulfur trioxide and why the predicted conditions are not all used in industry.

notes.h: Optimising yield: a general method (Higher Level only)
notes.b: For any equilibrium you can choose conditions the same way. First decide what favours the product, then weigh that against practical limits.
points: General method for any equilibrium: for the best yield choose the temperature that favours the exothermic or endothermic direction as needed, the pressure that favours the side with fewer (or more) gas moles, and an excess of a cheap reactant or removal of product.
Then weigh these choices against rate, cost, energy use and safety, because the best conditions for yield are rarely the best for the whole process.
Sustainability: lower temperatures and pressures save energy and reduce CO₂ emissions, and a good catalyst lets a process run at a lower temperature.
notes.tip: Industrial conditions are compromises. Say what Le Châtelier predicts, then give the reason (rate, cost, safety) that the real conditions differ.

notes.b: A reversible reaction that changes colour lets you see the position of equilibrium shift. This investigation tests Le Châtelier’s principle by changing one factor at a time.
points: Aim: to investigate how changes in concentration and temperature affect the position of an equilibrium, and to test whether the results agree with Le Châtelier’s principle.
Independent variable (the factor you deliberately change): here concentration or temperature.
Dependent variable (what you observe as a result): the colour of the equilibrium mixture, which shows the position of equilibrium; more of the coloured product gives a deeper colour.
Controlled variables (kept the same so the test is fair): the volume of solution, the number of drops added, the observer and the white background.

Set up one equilibrium mixture and divide it into equal portions in identical test tubes; keep one tube untouched as a control (a comparison with no change) and change one factor in each of the others.
Compare each tube with the control and record the colour before and after the change.
notes.tip: Use temperature-dependent examples (cobalt chloride, NO₂/N₂O₄) to describe a temperature experiment. Catalysts are not part of this investigation.

notes.h: Investigation: iron(III) chloride and potassium thiocyanate (concentration)
notes.b: This equilibrium is a good test of concentration changes because the product is strongly coloured. Adding or removing a reactant visibly changes the red colour.
points: Equation: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). Fe³⁺ (from iron(III) chloride) is yellow, SCN⁻ (from potassium thiocyanate) is colourless, and FeSCN²⁺ is blood-red.

Method: add about 1 cm³ of 0.1 M iron(III) chloride and 1 cm³ of 0.1 M potassium thiocyanate to about 100 cm³ of deionised water and stir; a pale red solution forms. Diluting it makes the colour changes easy to see.
Pour equal portions (about 10 cm³) into four test tubes; tube 1 is the control.
Tube 2: add a few drops of iron(III) chloride solution; the red deepens, because [Fe³⁺] (the concentration of Fe³⁺) increases and the equilibrium shifts to the right, forming more FeSCN²⁺.
Tube 3: add a few drops of potassium thiocyanate solution; the red deepens, because [SCN⁻] increases and the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Tube 4: add a few drops of silver nitrate solution; a white precipitate (an insoluble solid formed in a solution) forms and the red colour fades.

Silver ions remove SCN⁻ as insoluble silver thiocyanate, AgSCN, lowering [SCN⁻], so the equilibrium shifts to the left; silver chloride, also white, can form from the chloride ions in the iron(III) chloride.
Conclusion: adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right; removing a reactant shifts it to the left, as Le Châtelier’s principle predicts.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe how to set up this equilibrium, show the effect of a concentration change and explain the colour changes. Don’t state as a fixed fact whether heating deepens or fades the red; if a question gives the colour change on heating or cooling, deduce the shift, the sign of ΔH and the change in Kc from it.

notes.b: A labelled diagram sums up the four tubes and the colour each one shows.
points: Diagram: a row of four test tubes in a rack, labelled control, + FeCl₃, + KSCN and + AgNO₃, showing pale red, deep red, deep red, and pale or colourless with a white precipitate.

notes.b: The cobalt(II) chloride equilibrium shows both concentration and temperature effects, because its two forms are different colours and the forward reaction is endothermic.
points: Equation: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq) + 6H₂O(l).
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink and [CoCl₄]²⁻ is blue; the forward reaction is endothermic.
Method: dissolve a little cobalt(II) chloride in water to give a pink solution; add concentrated hydrochloric acid drop by drop until the solution is violet, a mixture of pink and blue.
Divide the violet solution into test tubes, keeping one as a control.
Adding more concentrated hydrochloric acid adds Cl⁻ and turns the solution blue: the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Adding water turns the solution pink: water is a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the left. Dilution also favours the side with more dissolved ions, here the left, with five ions against one.
notes.tip: Adding water to the cobalt chloride mixture is a change in concentration, not just dilution of colour. Exams ask for the colour change on adding concentrated HCl and on adding water.

notes.h: Cobalt(II) chloride: temperature, safety and diagram
notes.b: Because the forward reaction is endothermic, temperature changes move this equilibrium in a predictable direction. The chemicals involved need careful handling.
points: Heating: a tube placed in a beaker of hot water (about 80 °C) turns blue, because heating favours the endothermic forward reaction.
Cooling: a tube placed in ice-water turns pink, because cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction.
The changes reverse when the tubes return to room temperature, showing that the reaction is reversible and still dynamic.
Because heating shifts this equilibrium to the right, Kc for it increases with temperature.
Safety: concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive and gives off choking fumes, so wear goggles and gloves and work in a fume cupboard.
Safety: cobalt(II) chloride is toxic, may cause cancer and skin allergy, and is harmful to aquatic life, so wear gloves and put waste in the residue container, not the sink.

Diagram: three test tubes of the violet mixture, one in a beaker of hot water (blue), one in a beaker of ice-water (pink) and one at room temperature as a control (violet), with a thermometer in each beaker.
notes.tip: Exams ask the colour change on heating and cooling, and whether the reaction has stopped when the colour is constant. It has not: it is still dynamic. You may also be asked to deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and how Kc changes, from a colour change.

notes.h: Investigation: nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide (temperature, teacher demonstration)
notes.b: This gas equilibrium shows a temperature effect directly, because one form is brown and the other is colourless. The teacher performs it because NO₂ is toxic.
points: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), with the forward reaction exothermic; NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless.
Sealed glass tubes containing the same equilibrium mixture are placed in hot water and in ice-water.
The hot tube becomes darker brown, as the equilibrium shifts to the left, the endothermic direction, giving more NO₂.
The cold tube becomes paler, as the equilibrium shifts to the right.
Safety: NO₂ is very toxic; the tubes are sealed and the demonstration is done by the teacher.
Diagram: two sealed tubes, one in hot water and one in ice-water, each labelled with its colour.
notes.tip: Use temperature-dependent examples such as NO₂/N₂O₄ to describe a temperature experiment.

notes.b: Primary data are collected by you in the laboratory; secondary data come from somewhere else, such as a simulation, table or graph. Both can show how an equilibrium responds to a disturbance.
points: A digital simulation models the particles of a reversible reaction; the user can add reactant or product, or change the temperature, and watch the numbers of each particle and the forward and reverse rates change until a new equilibrium is set up.
Simulations show what cannot be seen in the laboratory: both reactions continuing at equal rates at equilibrium, and concentration–time graphs showing the sudden change and the new constant levels.
Simulations are safe, fast and repeatable and avoid toxic chemicals, but they are models: their results depend on the rules programmed into them, so they are checked against experimental data.
Secondary data, such as a table or graph of the percentage of ammonia at equilibrium at different temperatures and pressures, can be analysed for trends.
The percentage of ammonia rises with pressure and falls with temperature, so the forward reaction reduces the number of moles of gas and is exothermic.
On a concentration–time graph, a sudden vertical jump in one line shows a substance being added; the gradual changes that follow show the shift; new horizontal lines show the new equilibrium.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to give advantages and a limitation of a simulation, and to interpret percentage yield against temperature and pressure. Don’t name a particular simulation package.

notes.b: Judging a colour by eye is not exact, so the method is designed to make the comparison fair and the results reliable.
points: Judging colour by eye is subjective (it depends on the observer): compare each tube with the control against a white background, use the same volume in identical tubes, and have the same observer.
Add the same number of drops to each tube, and allow time for the new equilibrium to set up (the colour stops changing) before recording.
Concentration changes move the position of equilibrium but do not change Kc; temperature changes both.
Adding a solution also dilutes the mixture a little, so add only a few drops, or add the same volume of water to the control.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by moving in the direction that opposes the change.
The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium, which move when conditions change.
The movement of an equilibrium to the left or to the right in response to a disturbance.
Describes a reaction that releases heat to the surroundings and has a negative ΔH.
Describes a reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings and has a positive ΔH.
The amount of product obtained at equilibrium, compared with the maximum possible.
The temperature and pressure chosen in industry to balance yield, rate, cost and safety.
The untouched sample kept under the same conditions, against which the changed samples are compared.
The factor deliberately changed in an investigation, here concentration or temperature.
The quantity measured in response to the change, here the colour of the equilibrium mixture.
A factor kept the same in every test so that it cannot affect the result.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions react.
Data collected directly by the investigator from their own experiment.
Data collected by someone else, such as published tables or graphs, which can be analysed for trends.
A computer model of particles that shows how a reaction system behaves under chosen conditions.

questions.prompt: State Le Châtelier’s principle. For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −57 kJ mol⁻¹, predict and explain the effect on the colour of the mixture of (i) increasing the temperature, (ii) increasing the pressure, (iii) adding a catalyst.
questions.model: Le Châtelier’s principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system responds so as to oppose the change, and a new equilibrium is set up. (i) The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, the endothermic direction, which absorbs heat. More brown NO₂ forms, so the mixture becomes darker. (ii) Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas, which is N₂O₄ (1 mol, against 2 mol of NO₂). The mixture darkens at once because the concentration rises, then becomes paler as the equilibrium shifts to the right, but not as pale as before. (iii) A catalyst does not change the position of the equilibrium, so the colour does not change; it only allows equilibrium to be reached more quickly.

questions.prompt: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Use Le Châtelier’s principle to predict the temperature and pressure that give the greatest yield of ammonia, and explain why the conditions used industrially are a compromise. State the role of the iron catalyst.
questions.model: A high pressure gives the greatest yield: there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to reduce the pressure. A low temperature gives the greatest yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts to the right to release heat. Industrially a pressure of about 200 atm and a temperature of about 450 °C are used as a compromise. A higher pressure would give more ammonia, but a plant that can withstand it is very expensive to build and run, and the risk of leaks and explosions increases. At low temperature the reaction is too slow to be economic, so a temperature in the range 400–500 °C is used to give a reasonable yield at a fast enough rate. The iron catalyst does not change the yield; it allows equilibrium to be approached quickly at the compromise temperature. Ammonia is also removed by cooling and liquefying it, and unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.

questions.prompt: Explain, using Le Châtelier’s principle, why increasing levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere make it harder for shellfish to build their shells.
questions.model: Carbon dioxide dissolves in the sea: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq), and CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). More dissolved CO₂ increases the concentration of carbonic acid, which is a reactant in the equilibrium H₂CO₃(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) ⇌ 2HCO₃⁻(aq). Adding this reactant shifts that equilibrium to the right, so carbonate ions are used up. With less carbonate available, shellfish cannot build calcium carbonate shells as easily.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would set up an equilibrium between iron(III) ions and thiocyanate ions, and show the effect of changing the concentration of (i) a reactant added, (ii) a reactant removed. Explain each observation using Le Châtelier’s principle.
questions.model: Add about 1 cm³ of 0.1 M iron(III) chloride and 1 cm³ of 0.1 M potassium thiocyanate to about 100 cm³ of deionised water and stir; a pale red solution forms, containing the equilibrium Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). Pour equal portions of about 10 cm³ into four test tubes, keeping one as a control, and compare each tube with the control against a white background. (i) Add the same small number of drops of iron(III) chloride or potassium thiocyanate solution, a reactant added: the red colour deepens. The equilibrium shifts to the right to use up the added reactant, forming more FeSCN²⁺. (ii) Add a few drops of silver nitrate solution, which removes thiocyanate ions as a white precipitate of silver thiocyanate, AgSCN: the red colour fades. Removing a reactant lowers its concentration, so the equilibrium shifts to the left, forming less FeSCN²⁺.

questions.prompt: A violet solution contains the equilibrium [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O (pink ⇌ blue), with the forward reaction endothermic. State and explain the colour change when (i) the solution is cooled in ice-water, (ii) concentrated hydrochloric acid is added, (iii) water is added.
questions.model: (i) The solution turns pink. Cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction, so the equilibrium shifts to the left, forming more pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺. (ii) The solution turns blue. Concentrated hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions, a reactant, so the equilibrium shifts to the right, forming more blue [CoCl₄]²⁻. (iii) The solution turns pink. Adding water adds a product, so the equilibrium shifts to the left; dilution also favours the side with more dissolved ions, which is again the left.

questions.prompt: Give two advantages and one limitation of using a digital simulation instead of a laboratory experiment to investigate an equilibrium.
questions.model: Two advantages: simulations are safe, because no toxic or corrosive chemicals are handled, and they are fast and repeatable. Simulations also show the particles and the forward and reverse rates, which cannot be seen in the laboratory. One limitation: a simulation is a model, so its results depend on the rules programmed into it and must be checked against experimental data.
